title: Decimal Place Value Grade 5: Thousandths Made Clear + Free Quiz
meta_title: Decimal Place Value Grade 5 Thousandths + Quiz
meta_desc: Master decimal place value in Grade 5 to thousandths: read, write, expand, compare and order decimals on a number line, with a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: The jump from hundredths to thousandths is where a lot of Grade 5 students quietly lose the thread. Here is how the third decimal place actually works, plus a quick quiz to check your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 0.7, 0.70 and 0.700 on a board and ask a Grade 5 class whether they are the same number. Half will say yes, a confident few will say no, and one child will ask why we bother with the extra zeros at all. That single question is the whole of decimal place value grade 5 thousandths in a nutshell — once a student truly sees that the value of a digit depends on the column it sits in, the tenths, hundredths and thousandths places stop being a mystery. This is the skill NCERT builds toward after ‘Tenths and Hundredths’, and it is worth slowing down for.

In my experience teaching ten-year-olds, the third decimal place trips people up not because the maths is hard, but because the pattern from whole numbers suddenly runs in the opposite direction. Let me walk through how I teach it, in order.

The place-value chart, extended to thousandths

Everything starts with one chart. To the left of the decimal point the columns get ten times bigger as you move left; to the right they get ten times smaller as you move right. Tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. A thousandth is one part of something split into 1,000 equal pieces — think of one rupee shared into 1,000, so each share is ₹0.001.

HundredsTensOnes.TenthsHundredthsThousandths
100101.1/101/1001/1000
3.456

Read the bottom row as three and four hundred fifty-six thousandths, or 3.456. The 4 is worth 0.4, the 5 is worth 0.05, and the 6 is worth 0.006. Notice the trap the columns set: the 6 looks bigger than the 4, but sitting in the thousandths place makes it the smallest of the three. Position beats appearance every time.

Reading and writing decimals to three places

Once the chart is solid, reading a decimal aloud becomes a routine. Say the whole-number part, say ‘and’ for the point, then read the decimal part as if it were a whole number followed by the name of the last column.

  • 0.7 → ‘seven tenths’
  • 0.07 → ‘seven hundredths’
  • 0.007 → ‘seven thousandths’
  • 2.305 → ‘two and three hundred five thousandths’

The zeros matter enormously here. In 2.305 the zero holds the hundredths column open so the 5 lands in thousandths. Drop it and you get 2.35, a completely different number. This is the one place I tell students never to be lazy about writing a zero.

The zeros that do and do not matter

Trailing zeros after the last non-zero digit — the ones in 0.700 — do not change the value, because they add nothing to a column that already reads zero. So 0.7, 0.70 and 0.700 really are equal. But a zero between the point and a digit, as in 0.07, is a placeholder doing real work. Teaching that distinction clears up most of the confusion in one lesson.

Expanded form of a decimal

Expanded form makes the value of each digit visible, which is exactly why it is worth the effort. Break a decimal into the sum of what each digit is worth:

3.456 = 3 + 0.4 + 0.05 + 0.006, or with fractions, 3 + 4/10 + 5/100 + 6/1000.

Students who can move between the standard form, the expanded form and the fraction form have genuinely understood place value rather than memorised a procedure. I ask for all three every time in the first week.

Comparing and ordering decimals

Here is the counter-intuitive bit that catches many children: a longer decimal is not always the bigger one. A student who thinks 0.45 is smaller than 0.9 ‘because 45 is more than 9’ has fallen for the digit-count trap. The fix is to compare column by column, left to right, and to line up the decimal points.

StepWhat to doExample: 0.45 vs 0.9
1Line up decimal points0.45 and 0.90
2Add zeros so lengths match0.45 and 0.90
3Compare tenths first4 tenths vs 9 tenths
4Decide0.9 is bigger

Rewriting 0.9 as 0.90 is the move that makes it obvious. Once the tenths column decides the winner, you never even reach the hundredths. Only when two decimals tie in a column do you move right to the next one.

Decimals on a number line

A number line turns all this abstraction into distance you can point at. To place 0.456, first find the whole-number gap it lives in — between 0 and 1. Split that gap into ten to find the tenths, so 0.456 sits between 0.4 and 0.5. Split that smaller gap into ten again for hundredths, and once more for thousandths. Each zoom is the same ‘divide by ten’ idea repeating.

I like this because it quietly answers the ordering question too: whichever decimal sits further right on the line is the larger one. Number sense and comparison become the same picture.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these ideas — place value to thousandths, reading and writing decimals, expanded form, comparing, and the number line. Let your child work through it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Decimal Place Value Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on tenths, hundredths and thousandths — reading, writing, expanded form, comparing and the number line. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 decimal place value to thousandths

questions.q: In the number 3.456, what is the value of the digit 5?
questions.explanation: The 5 sits in the hundredths column, so its value is 5 hundredths, which is 0.05.

questions.q: How do you write 'seven thousandths' as a decimal?
questions.explanation: Thousandths is the third place after the point, so seven thousandths is 0.007.
Compare tenths first. 0.9 has 9 tenths; the others have only 4 tenths. So 0.9 is largest.

questions.q: What is 2 + 0.3 + 0.05 + 0.006 written in standard form?
questions.explanation: Place each digit in its column: 3 tenths, 5 hundredths, 6 thousandths gives 2.356.

questions.q: Which of these is equal to 0.6?
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros after the last digit do not change the value, so 0.600 equals 0.6.

questions.q: In 0.208, what is the value of the digit 8?
questions.explanation: The 8 is in the third place after the point, the thousandths column, so it is 8 thousandths.

questions.q: Order these from smallest to largest: 0.5, 0.05, 0.505
questions.explanation: Line up the points: 0.050, 0.500, 0.505. Comparing columns gives 0.05, then 0.5, then 0.505.

questions.q: On a number line, 0.456 lies between which two numbers?
questions.explanation: The tenths digit is 4, so 0.456 sits in the gap between 0.4 and 0.5.

faq.q: What is the thousandths place in decimals?
faq.a: It is the third digit after the decimal point. It shows how many parts you have when something is split into 1,000 equal pieces, so 0.001 is one thousandth. In 3.456 the digit 6 is in the thousandths place and is worth 0.006.

Yes. Trailing zeros after the last non-zero digit do not add any value, because they sit in columns that already read zero. So 0.7, 0.70 and 0.700 are all equal — only zeros that hold a place open, like the one in 0.07, change the number.

Compare column by column from the left, not by counting digits. Line them up as 0.45 and 0.90. The tenths column has 4 against 9, so 0.9 wins before you even look at the hundredths. A longer decimal is not automatically the larger one.

faq.q: What is expanded form of a decimal?
faq.a: It writes a decimal as the sum of what each digit is worth. For example, 3.456 = 3 + 0.4 + 0.05 + 0.006, or 3 + 4/10 + 5/100 + 6/1000. It makes place value visible and is a great check that a child really understands the columns.
